# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: MUTE

You hold the manual. You cannot speak, you never see the bomb, and you cannot touch it.

## Your channels

When you gesture, Deaf receives it.
You cannot speak.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

I'm the Mute — the manual is mine, and my only output channel is gestures that only the Deaf can see. Let me map the topology before I send anything:

- **Me (Mute) → Deaf**, via gesture. That is my entire reach.
- **Deaf → everyone**, via voice: the Deaf can speak to the Blind and to me.
- **Blind → everyone**, via voice: the Blind can hear me not at all (I'm silent), but can hear Deaf, and can speak to Deaf and to me.

So the Deaf is the router of this team: whatever I know must pass through Deaf's mouth to reach the hands that can actually work the bomb. My manual is a lookup table — a display number crossed with a light colour gives a colour. Someone with eyes has to read the display and the light off the bomb, I look it up, and the answer has to travel back by voice to the Blind.

The hard part is the bootstrap: my gestures mean nothing yet. But some gestures carry natural meaning a sighted monkey will read correctly on first sight: 👋 (hello — I am signalling you), 🤌 (the classic "what?" — I need information from you), 👍/👎 (yes/no — a confirmation channel), 🙏 (please). The Deaf also already knows the roles: Mute holds the manual. So the Deaf should expect exactly this: the manual-holder asking to be told what the bomb looks like, and offering a yes/no channel for answers.

My opening move is to establish contact, request the bomb's visible state, and pre-agree the thumbs-up/thumbs-down convention so the Deaf can start polling me for lookups next round instead of guessing at my signals.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👋", "🫵", "🤌"])
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍", "👎", "🙏"])
```

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Blind says to Mute: Blind here, hands only. My inventory: one display, one light, and seven wires at positions 1 to 7. Touch gives me no colours, no markings, no displayed text, so every value on my board is blank to me. Please read the manual and tell me in plain words what it keys on and which wire it wants cut. Two warnings: Deaf cannot hear you, so gesture anything meant for Deaf; and Deaf CAN speak aloud, but we only hear it a round later. Ask Deaf to describe the display, the light, and all seven wire colours out loud, in order, position by position.
Blind gestures: [👋 👍 👎]
Deaf says: Deaf here. I see everything, I hear nothing. To both of you: the display reads 1. The light is orange. There are seven wires, in order: position 1 white, 2 blue, 3 orange, 4 red, 5 purple, 6 yellow, 7 green. That is everything I can see. Proposed code, because your only way to answer me is with hand signs, which I can see: thumbs up means yes, thumbs down means no, a wave means hello or acknowledged, one pointing-up finger repeated means a count, so three taps means three, pinched fingers means question or 'what', folded hands means please or hurry. Mute: I received your waves, hello, and yes, I can see the bomb clearly. Check your manual for a module with a display reading 1, an orange light and seven coloured wires, and sign me what it says using the code above. If anything must reach Blind from the manual, sign it to me and I will say it out loud. Blind: I can see your signs, so feel the bomb and report the same way — tap a pointing finger once for each wire you can count, thumbs up or down for yes or no, and sign me anything else you can feel that I have not listed: buttons, panels, seams, screws.
Deaf gestures to Mute: [👋 👍 🤌]

Let me work the lookup first, because everything hinges on it. The manual is a table: display value down the side, light colour across the top, and the cell gives a colour. Deaf reports display **1**, light **orange**. Row 1, column orange → **green**. The natural reading of a defusal table keyed on display and light, with seven distinctly-coloured wires, is: cut the wire of the resulting colour. Deaf's own list tells me where green lives: positions 1–7 are white, blue, orange, red, purple, yellow, green — green appears exactly once, at **position 7**.

The elegant part: I never need to transmit the word "green". Deaf and Blind both know the wires by position; the colour is only an intermediate step that Deaf's list has already resolved. So my payload is just "cut seven".

For encoding, I stand in Deaf's shoes: we agreed that repeated ☝ is a count, so seven ☝ taps is seven. For "cut" I send ✌ — it reads as scissors, the one hand shape in the alphabet that carries "cut" on first sight. I split it into separate calls so the seven taps can't be misread as one blob of eight symbols, and I close with 🙏, which Deaf defined as please/hurry, to mark this as the actionable answer, urgent.

I expect Deaf to relay this aloud to Blind as "cut the wire at position 7" next round, and ideally to repeat it back to me — if Deaf signs it back, I'll confirm with 👍. If the display or light changes after the cut, I'll need Deaf to re-report both for a fresh lookup; that protocol can wait one round.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✌"])
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["☝", "☝", "☝", "☝", "☝", "☝", "☝"])
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["🙏"])
```

Deaf's recitation is a perfect match against my manual, cell for cell — all five rows, all five columns, no errors. That means thumbs up, and with it the display-8-blue→red→position-4 lookup is validated too; Blind should already be cutting. What remains are the three edge questions, and honesty matters more than comfort here: my manual contains *only* the 5×5 table. There is no prose anywhere — no provision for a cut colour that's no longer present, no rule for a display value outside {1,3,4,8,9} or a light outside the five columns, and no stated end condition. So the answer to all three is the same: the manual is silent.

Silence in a defusal manual is dangerous, though — an undefined state is exactly where a wrong guess detonates the bomb. So I spell not just the answers but the policy that follows from them: any state the table can't reach means stop, do not guess. Since Deaf now holds the full table, the per-cut dependency on me is gone; my role going forward is verification and edge-case judgment, which only works if Deaf knows the table's boundaries are hard.
